DOCUMENT:
Pricing Proposal: Introducing an Off-Peak Membership
Pulse Fitness, Commercial Team, August 2026

1. Proposal
We propose introducing an off-peak membership at £29 a month from 1 October 2026, alongside our existing standard membership at £42 a month. Off-peak members would have access before 4 pm on weekdays and all day at weekends, with full access to the gym floor and to classes running in those hours.

2. Background
Pulse operates four clubs with 9,600 standard members. Membership has been flat for 18 months, while two budget gyms have opened within our catchments, both offering memberships at £22 to £25 a month. Our clubs are busy between 5 pm and 8 pm on weekdays, when the gym floor often runs at or near capacity, but quiet during weekday daytimes, when typical utilisation is around 30%.

Access-control data for May to July 2026 show that 31% of our current standard members visit exclusively in what would be the off-peak window, and a further 22% visit mostly off-peak.

3. Market evidence
A survey of 640 non-members living within two miles of our clubs, conducted in June, found that 19% would "definitely" or "probably" join at £29 a month for off-peak access. The most interested groups were retirees, shift workers, parents of school-age children and students.

Four of our six closest competitors already offer an off-peak or daytime membership, priced between £25 and £32.

4. Classes and retention
Retention is the other half of our commercial challenge. Monthly churn among members who attend at least one class a week is 2.1%, against 4.8% among members who do not attend classes. Classes clearly keep members loyal, so we will add six extra daytime classes per club each week to support the new membership, which should lower churn among off-peak members towards the 2.1% level. The additional classes would cost £18,700 a month across the four clubs in instructor fees.

5. Revenue projection
We expect to recruit 1,200 new off-peak members in the first year, about 300 per club, which is consistent with the survey response and the size of our catchments. At £29 a month, this is £34,800 a month, or £417,600 a year, in new membership revenue. After the cost of the additional classes (£224,400 a year), net additional revenue is £193,200 a year.

Because daytime utilisation is low, the additional members can be accommodated without investment in equipment or space.

6. Operational changes
Access control will be updated so that off-peak members' cards do not open the turnstiles outside their access window. Off-peak members will have weekday access until 5 pm, giving those finishing early shifts or school pick-ups time to train. Members will be able to upgrade to standard membership at any time, and to switch between membership types with one month's notice.

7. Risks
Some standard members may perceive the off-peak price as unfair. We will communicate the change as an extension of choice. Competitor responses are possible; the budget gyms already price below our proposed off-peak rate, so we do not expect a price war.

8. Staff consultation
Club managers and front-of-house teams at all four clubs were consulted in July. Managers supported the proposal, noting that daytime classes are often under-filled and that a daytime membership would help build a regular community at quieter times. Front-of-house staff asked for clear signage and app messaging about access hours, which we will provide before launch.

9. Recommendation
The off-peak membership fills spare daytime capacity, responds to competitor offers and targets clearly identified customer groups. We project net additional revenue of around £193,000 a year and recommend launch on 1 October 2026.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Off-peak members will have weekday access until 5 pm" -- Section 1 defines off-peak access as before 4 pm on weekdays; section 6 says off-peak members have weekday access until 5 pm (also into the busy 5-8 pm period the document says is near capacity). The access window contradicts itself.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "Classes clearly keep members loyal, so we will add six extra daytime classes per club each week" -- The churn difference is correlational: members who choose to attend classes weekly are likely more engaged/committed to begin with (self-selection). It does not show classes cause lower churn, nor that adding classes would bring off-peak churn to 2.1%.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "At £29 a month, this is £34,800 a month, or £417,600 a year, in new membership revenue." -- The projection counts only new members and ignores downgrades, although the document states 31% of the 9,600 standard members (about 2,976) already visit only off-peak and can switch with one month's notice. If they downgraded, revenue would fall by about £13 x 2,976 = £38,700 a month (about £464,000 a year), more than wiping out the projected gain.

REVIEW:
# Review: Off-Peak Membership Proposal

The proposal is clearly written and the arithmetic is internally correct (£34,800 × 12 = £417,600; £18,700 × 12 = £224,400; difference £193,200). But the projection leaves out the largest financial effect, and several of the supporting arguments are weaker than the author's summary claims. As written, the "low-risk, ~£193k net" conclusion is not supported.

## 1. The projection ignores cannibalisation, which likely outweighs all the new revenue

Section 2 says **31% of standard members visit exclusively in the off-peak window**, and another 22% visit mostly off-peak. The proposal never connects this to the revenue projection.

- 31% × 9,600 = **~2,976 members** who would lose nothing by moving to the £29 tier.
- Each one who downgrades costs £13 a month. If all of them do, that is **~£38,700 a month, or ~£464,000 a year**.
- That exceeds the entire £417,600 gross from new members. Even before class costs, the scheme would lose money.
- Section 6 makes switching easy ("switch between membership types with one month's notice"). Some of the 22% "mostly off-peak" group will also downgrade.

Even partial take-up is costly. If only half the exclusive off-peak group switches, the loss is ~£232,000 a year, which would more than eliminate the £193,200 net. The Risks section (7) mentions perceived unfairness but not this revenue loss. This is the central omission. The proposal needs a downgrade scenario analysis, or a design that limits downgrades, before it can be called low-risk.

## 2. The access window is inconsistent and conflicts with the capacity argument

- Section 1 gives access **before 4 pm**.
- Section 6 gives access **until 5 pm**.

The 5 pm version runs into the stated 5–8 pm peak, when the floor is "at or near capacity." The 4–5 pm hour is likely busy as well. Also, the capacity evidence (around 30% utilisation) covers **weekday daytimes only**, yet the product includes **all-day weekend access**. Weekend utilisation is never reported, so "no investment in equipment or space" is unsupported for weekends.

## 3. The 1,200-member forecast is asserted, not derived

- The survey reports 19% of 640 respondents saying "definitely" or "probably." Stated purchase intent, especially "probably," usually converts at a small fraction of the stated rate. No conversion assumption is applied.
- The proposal never states the catchment population. So "consistent with the survey response and the size of our catchments" cannot be checked, and calling 300 per club "conservative" or "well within what the survey implies" has no visible basis.
- The survey appears to have tested £29 off-peak alone. Respondents were not asked to weigh it against the **£22–25 full-access budget gyms** nearby.

## 4. The revenue arithmetic assumes 1,200 members for the full year with no churn

£417,600 assumes all 1,200 members pay for all 12 months. In practice:

- Recruitment ramps up over the year, so first-year revenue would be much lower. Average membership might be roughly half the year-end figure.
- Churn is not applied. Even at the optimistic 2.1% a month, about 22% of members would leave within a year. At 4.8%, about 45% would.

Meanwhile the class costs (£18,700 a month) start in full from launch. First-year net is therefore materially overstated, even before cannibalisation is counted.

## 5. The retention argument confuses correlation with causation

Class attenders churning at 2.1% versus 4.8% for non-attenders does not show that classes *cause* retention. More engaged members are both more likely to attend classes and less likely to leave. Expecting off-peak churn to fall "towards the 2.1% level" because classes are added is unsupported. Calling the £224,400 a year an "investment in keeping new members" depends entirely on that causal claim.

## 6. Section 8 undercuts the case for extra classes

Club managers say "daytime classes are **often under-filled**." That suggests there is already spare daytime class capacity. It is unclear why six *additional* classes per club per week, at £224,400 a year, are needed. Filling existing classes would be cheaper. This line item is the main cost in the projection and needs justification.

## 7. The competitive reasoning is weak

Section 7 argues that because budget gyms "already price below our proposed off-peak rate, we do not expect a price war." This reverses the real risk. Budget rivals offer **full access for less than Pulse's restricted product**. Price-sensitive groups such as students and retirees may still choose them. The competitor comparison in Section 3 uses the six closest competitors' off-peak prices (£25–32), which is a different benchmark from the budget gyms named in Section 2 as the cause of flat membership.

## 8. Smaller points

- **Upgrade and switching terms:** "Upgrade at any time" sits alongside "switch with one month's notice." It should be clear which applies to downgrades, since that rule directly controls the cannibalisation exposure.
- **Effect on standard members:** Adding off-peak members alongside daytime-heavy standard members could crowd popular daytime classes. This is not assessed.
- **Launch date:** The document targets 1 October 2026, which has now passed. If it is being revisited, the timeline and figures should be refreshed.

## Suggested revisions

1. Model downgrades from the 31% and 22% groups under several take-up scenarios and net them against new revenue. Consider limiting the risk, for example by making the tier available to new members only for a period, or by narrowing the window.
2. Fix the access window, keep it clear of 5 pm, and provide weekend utilisation data.
3. Show the catchment population and the intent-to-purchase conversion behind the 1,200 figure.
4. Phase recruitment and apply churn in the first-year projection.
5. Justify the extra classes given that existing daytime classes are under-filled, or drop or reduce them.
6. Add cannibalisation and the budget-gym full-access comparison to the Risks section.

As it stands, the proposal does not support its recommendation. Once existing members' downgrades are counted, the likely outcome is a net loss rather than a gain of around £193,000.
